name: King's Indian Defense: Mar del Plata Variation
summary: King's Indian Mar del Plata: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 Ne7, the opposite-wing pawn-storm main line.
intro: The Mar del Plata Variation is the archetypal King's Indian battleground, reached after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 Ne7. With 8.d5 the centre locks and the two sides commit to attacks on opposite wings. White expands on the queenside while Black launches a direct kingside pawn storm aimed at the white king. It is one of the most thematic and uncompromising structures in all of chess, deeply theoretical, richly double-edged, and famous for its all-or-nothing racing character.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 O-O Nc6 d5 Ne7

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining feature is the closed centre after 8.d5. Because the pawn chains point in opposite directions, White's natural play flows to the queenside and Black's to the kingside, producing a race in which both sides attack the enemy king. White plays c5 and b4, opens lines with cxd6 or a well-timed pawn break, and invades on the c-file and the queenside light squares. Black, whose knight has retreated to e7 to clear the f-pawn's path, plays ...Ng6 or ...Nd7, then ...f5, ...f4, ...g5-g4 and ...h5, rolling the kingside pawns forward to open lines against White's king. Tempo is everything.

Both attacks are structurally justified, so success usually depends on speed and precision rather than material. Black often sacrifices pawns or even pieces to prise open the g- and h-files, aiming for mating attacks, while White races to break through on c7 and the queenside before Black's storm arrives. Key squares include c5 and c7 for White and f4, g4 and h3 for Black. The bishop on g7, blunted by its own e5-pawn, can spring to life if the centre ever opens. Because both plans are so committal, small differences in move order and timing frequently decide the game.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: From the tabiya after 8...Ne7, the main branching point is White's ninth move. 9.Ne1 is the classic retreat, clearing the way for f3 and the queenside advance with Nd3, c5 and b4, while stopping ...Ng4. 9.Nd2 pursues a similar plan and supports the c4-c5 break. The sharp 9.b4 speeds up White's queenside play, and 9.Bd2 with a3 and b4 is another mainstream route. Against all of these Black proceeds with ...Ne8 or ...Nd7, ...f5 and the thematic kingside pawn storm, and the resulting positions are among the most heavily analysed in opening theory.

After the standard 9.Ne1 Nd7 (or 9...Ne8) 10.f3 f5, play typically continues 11.g4 or 11.c5, each freezing part of the board while accelerating the player's own attack. A recurring debate concerns whether Black should meet g4 with ...f4 to lock the kingside and prepare ...g5-g4, or keep the tension. White meanwhile pushes c5 and looks to open the c-file with cxd6 and Nc4-b6 ideas. The battle often reduces to who arrives first: if White breaks through on the queenside the endgame favours him, while if Black's pawns crash through, mating attacks decide matters quickly.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation takes its name from the Argentine resort of Mar del Plata, where several influential King's Indian games in this structure were played in the mid-twentieth century, and it is also known as the Aronin-Taimanov Variation after two of its early practitioners. It became the proving ground for the King's Indian revival led by players such as Bronstein and Boleslavsky, and later Fischer, Kasparov and Radjabov, all of whom trusted Black's kingside attack against White's queenside space. It remains a benchmark of dynamic chess, endlessly analysed yet still fertile ground for new ideas.
